nameStory: The 'greedy' in this snail's name likely refers to its feeding behavior as a predatory mollusk that actively hunts other small marine creatures. Like many dove snails, these little hunters are surprisingly aggressive for their size, earning them this unflattering but memorable moniker. The 'dove' part comes from the family name, possibly referring to their generally small, rounded shells that early naturalists thought resembled a dove's gentle form.
description: The Greedy Dove Snail is a tiny predatory sea snail that lives in New England's coastal waters. These small marine gastropods (snails that crawl on their belly-foot) have compact, spiral shells that are typically less than half an inch long. They're carnivorous hunters despite their small size, feeding on other tiny marine organisms. As members of the dove snail family, they have relatively thick, sturdy shells compared to their diminutive size.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Compact, cone-shaped spiral shell that feels solid and heavy for its tiny size, usually shorter than your pinky fingernail

idTips.label: Shell Surface
idTips.description: Smooth to slightly textured shell surface that may feel glassy when wet, often with subtle spiral lines you can feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Shell Opening
idTips.description: Narrow, elongated opening (aperture) with a thick, rounded outer lip that feels sturdy to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small - typically less than 12mm (half an inch) long, easily fitting on a dime with room to spare

idTips.label: Body
idTips.description: When alive, extends a muscular foot and tentacles from the shell opening, retracts quickly when disturbed

habitat: Found in shallow coastal waters of New England, typically in rocky intertidal zones and subtidal areas with hard surfaces. They prefer areas with plenty of small prey organisms and often live among seaweed, under rocks, or attached to pier pilings and other marine structures. You're most likely to spot them during low tide in tide pools or washed up in beach wrack.

seasonality.spring: Active in warming waters, often more visible during spring low tides as they hunt for prey in tide pools.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season when they're most active and easiest to find during tide pool exploration.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may be found deeper as water temperatures begin to drop, look for shells washed up after storms.
seasonality.winter: Least active period, mostly found as empty shells on beaches or in deeper water where temperatures are more stable.

funFact: Despite being smaller than most people's thumbnail, Greedy Dove Snails are voracious predators that can drill tiny holes through other snails' shells using a specialized rasping tongue called a radula - they're basically microscopic shell-drilling pirates of the tide pools!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small marine snails found in tide pools, but the Greedy Dove Snail's compact, heavy-feeling shell and narrow opening help distinguish it from rounder periwinkles or more delicate-shelled species. Memory trick: 'Greedy and weighty' - the shell feels surprisingly solid for something so small.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'avara' actually means 'greedy' in Latin, so both the common and scientific names emphasize this snail's voracious appetite. With only 11 recorded observations in New England, this is considered a relatively uncommon species in our region, making any sighting noteworthy for citizen science projects.
compareHints: The Greedy Dove Snail differs from its close relative, the Well-ribbed Dove Snail, primarily in shell sculpture - the Well-ribbed species has much more prominent spiral ridges that you can easily feel with your finger, while the Greedy Dove Snail's shell surface is relatively smooth. Both are similarly sized, but the ribbing difference is usually obvious even in worn specimens.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Greedy Dove Snail, the Well-ribbed Dove Snail has much more prominent spiral ribs that create a noticeably bumpy texture you can feel with your fingertip.
